# Course workflow — issues, PRs, reviews, sprint deliverables

Course rules, not upstream Gitea ones. Source: the course site <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>
(Sprints pages) and `docs/sprint0/standards.md`. Everyone on the team, and every AI session, uses
the formats below so all issues and PRs look the same. The GitHub templates in `.github/` carry the
same formats; if they ever disagree with this page, fix the template.

AI disclosure has its own page: `AI-ASSISTANCE.md`.

## Current sprint: Sprint 2

- **Dates:** Oct 13 – Oct 29, 2026. Everything pushed and merged by **Oct 29, 11:59 PM**, except
  the D7 check-in, due **Oct 22, 11:59 PM**.
- **Points:** 100.
- **Zero rule:** no merged PR (D4), no sprint report (D8) or no release (D9) means **0 for the
  whole sprint**.
- **Carries forward:** anything the Sprint 2 page doesn't change comes from the Sprint 1 page, and
  every Sprint 0 standard still applies.

| # | Deliverable | Points | Who | Where |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | Sprint backlog: a `Sprint 2` milestone with every selected issue on it | 10 | Team | GitHub milestone |
| D2 | Requirements spec for each issue (formats below), peer-reviewed by a teammate before coding | 20 | Individual | Issue body |
| D3 | At least one non-trivial design decision per issue, with **at least two alternatives** | 5 | Individual | Issue body |
| D4 | Code changes and PRs, each with a `## Tech Debt` section | 20 | Individual | PRs |
| D5 | AI logs | 5 | Individual | `ai-logs/sprint2/<github-username>/` |
| D6 | UML class and sequence diagrams plus Q&A for one medium issue you resolved | 15 | Individual | `docs/sprint2/diagrams/` |
| D7 | Mid-sprint check-in | 5 | Individual | `docs/sprint2/checkin/<github-username>.md` |
| D8 | Sprint report | 10 | Team | `docs/sprint2/report.md` |
| D9 | Release: tag `v1.27.3-csci435-s2` plus a GitHub release | 2 | Team | Tags / Releases |
| D10 | Reflection survey | 8 | Individual | Blackboard/Zulip link |

- **D1 load:** each CSCI 435 student owns at least 2 medium issues; each CSCI 535 student owns at
  least 2 medium and 1 small. Either load can be met with equivalent story points instead. Every
  issue has exactly **one** assignee. Unfinished Sprint 1 issues
  go into the backlog before new work. To skip one, write the reason on that issue (closed, made
  invalid by later changes, or no longer relevant).
- **D3:** each decision names at least two concrete alternatives and why one won; this is graded
  strictly. The site also accepts the decision in an issue comment or the PR description; the team
  keeps it in the issue body. Decisions that span issues go in `docs/sprint2/design.md`.
- **D4:** every PR description has the Tech Debt section (see "Pull request format"). A PR without
  it loses points.
- **D5:** conventions are in `ai-logs/README.md`. Logs hold the full prompts and output: summaries,
  screenshots and share links are not logs. The link must open the log file itself, not a folder or
  another issue. The folder must exist even if no AI was used; in that case, post a comment saying
  so. The site accepts the link in an issue or a PR comment this sprint; the team keeps it in
  **issue comments only** (`AI-ASSISTANCE.md`).
- **D6:** see "UML diagrams (D6)" below.
- **D7:** about 150 words on each of: what you have done and what remains; one thing you learned
  about the codebase or about software engineering; one thing you would do differently. Late or
  thin scores 3 of 5.
- **D9:** keep the base version (`v1.27.3-csci435-s1` → `v1.27.3-csci435-s2`), tag after every
  Sprint 2 PR is merged, push the tag to origin, and write release notes listing the features,
  fixes and improvements. The site's example says `v2.17.2`; this fork's base is `v1.27.3`.
- **Reviews:** nobody approves or merges their own PR. Reviewers leave substantive comments, not a
  bare approval. Tell the reviewer on Zulip or by email, and aim to review within 24 hours. Each
  student reviews at least one PR per sprint, and every teammate at least once per semester.
- **Extra credit:** up to 3 points per PR accepted by upstream Gitea.

## Branches and commits

- Branches: `feat/issue-<N>-short-description`, `fix/issue-<N>-short-description` or
  `chore/short-description` (`STUDENTS.md`). One issue per branch.
- Commit messages follow Conventional Commits and end with the issue number:
  `feat(repo): show empty state on releases page (#17)`. Add an
  `Assisted-by: AGENT_NAME:MODEL_VERSION` trailer when AI helped; never `Co-Authored-By` or
  `Signed-off-by` (`AGENTS.md`). A human approves every commit before it is made.

### Before each implementation: sync with main

Every new branch starts from an up-to-date `main`. AI sessions run this before writing any code:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git switch -c feat/issue-<N>-short-description
```

To pick up new work on `main` for a branch that already exists, **merge, don't rebase**. Rebasing
or squashing after review has started is not allowed (`docs/sprint0/standards.md`):

```bash
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
```

Do this before opening the PR and again if `main` moves while it is in review. Never merge another
feature branch into yours.

### After merge: clean up

A PR is merged with a merge commit once it is approved, every review comment is addressed and CI
passes. Then:

```bash
git switch main
git pull origin main
git branch -d feat/issue-<N>-short-description               # local branch
git push origin --delete feat/issue-<N>-short-description    # or GitHub's "Delete branch" button
git fetch --prune                                            # drop stale remote-tracking refs
```

Also check that the issue closed (via `Closes #N`), is on the sprint milestone, and has its AI
Assistance comment. Then run `specstory sync` and file the session's log (see `ai-logs/README.md`).

## Issue format: feature (user story)

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user-story.yaml`. The user story must meet INVEST: Independent,
Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

```markdown
## User Story
As a <role>, I want <capability> so that <benefit>.

## User Scenario
<A short concrete walk-through: who, where in the UI, what they do, what they see.>

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given <state>, when <action>, then <observable result>.
- [ ] AC2: ...
- [ ] AC3: ...            (at least 3; each has a clear pass/fail result)

## Out of Scope
- <What this issue deliberately does not do.>

## Open Questions
- <Unresolved questions, or "None".>

## Design Decision
**Decision:** <what was chosen>
**Alternatives Considered:** <at least two concrete options, and why each lost>
**Rationale:** <why this one>
**Consequences:** <trade-offs, follow-up work, what it makes harder>

## Scope
small | medium | large, and matching `scope:` label
```

## Issue format: bug report

Template: `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/bug-report.yaml`.

```markdown
## Observed Behavior
## Expected Behavior
## Steps to Reproduce
1. ...
## Additional Information
<Version or commit, browser/OS, logs, screenshots.>
## Design Decision
<Same four fields as above: Decision, Alternatives Considered, Rationale, Consequences.>
```

- **Design Decision (D3):** fill it in once you've picked an approach, before opening the PR. Put
  a second decision under another `### Decision 2` heading. If a PR changes the decision, update
  the issue body.
- **Peer review (D2):** a teammate reads the spec and comments `Spec reviewed — <notes>` on the
  issue before implementation starts.

## Pull request format

Template: `.github/pull_request_template.md`. Title uses Conventional Commits, e.g.
`fix(issues): keep label filter after search`. Description sections:

1. `Closes #<N>`, which links the issue and closes it on merge.
2. **What changed:** the change in your own words.
3. **Why:** the problem, and which acceptance criteria (AC1…) it satisfies.
4. **How it was tested / Test strategy:** tests added or updated and why these ones. Name any
   change that can't be tested automatically and how it was checked by hand. Every behaviour change
   needs a new or updated test.
5. **CI / manual verification:** CI status, or the commands run and their results.
6. **Design:** one line pointing at the Design Decision in the issue, or a note on how it changed.
7. **Tech Debt:** required from Sprint 2. Both fields are required, and `None.` is a valid answer:

   ```markdown
   ## Tech Debt

   **Introduced:** <shortcuts, workarounds or design compromises this PR makes, and why>

   **Encountered:** <tech debt that was already there and that you ran into, and how you handled it>
   ```

8. **AI assistance:** format in `AI-ASSISTANCE.md` §2, with **no log link**.

Per-PR grading (20 points): correctness against the acceptance criteria 6, test strategy with
explanation 5, description quality including the Tech Debt section 4, CI or manual verification 3,
review rubric posted 2.

## Code review rubric

The reviewer posts this as a **PR comment**, as well as the GitHub review itself. A copy-paste copy
is in `.github/code-review-rubric.md`, so keep the two in sync. Pull the branch and test it when you
can, say what you checked, and mark each point as required or optional
(`docs/community-governance.md`). Score each row against the issue's acceptance criteria. Anything
below 7 needs a note saying what would raise it.

```markdown
### Code Review — @reviewer-username

**Checked:** <what you ran or tried>

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | | |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | | |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | | |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | | |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | | |
| Overall — merge as-is? | | |
```

## UML diagrams (D6)

The person who resolved a medium issue draws a class diagram and a sequence diagram for it. Several
small issues that together equal one medium issue are drawn together instead. Files:

- `docs/sprint2/diagrams/<issue#>-<github-username>-class.png` (or `.pdf`)
- `docs/sprint2/diagrams/<issue#>-<github-username>-sequence.png` (or `.pdf`)
- `docs/sprint2/diagrams/<issue#>-<github-username>.md`, which embeds both and answers the Q&A

What the diagrams need:

- Show the existing code found during concept location and impact analysis, and the new or changed
  code, and tell the two apart with a legend, colour or label.
- Show only the fields and methods that matter to the issue.
- Annotate the diagrams with the key design decisions and calls. Diagrams without annotations lose
  points.
- Add a short note on how Go maps to UML: structs, interfaces, and embedding.
- The `.md` follows the course template: `# Issue #<N> -- <title>`, `## Class Diagram`,
  `## Sequence Diagram`, `## Q&A`. The Q&A has 3 class-diagram questions, 3 sequence-diagram
  questions and 1 question on AI use, answered "N/A" if no AI was used. Copy the questions from the
  Sprint 2 page.

Grading (15 points): existing code 2, solution code 2, annotations 3, UML notation 2, Q&A 4, AI
transparency 2.

## Sprint report (D8) sections

`docs/sprint<N>/report.md`, following `docs/sprint0/report.md`:

- Team: names, GitHub usernames, project name, repository link.
- Sprint overview.
- Backlog: milestone link, why the team chose these issues, plus a table of title, owner, points,
  scope and status.
- Requirements and design: when specs were done, what surprised you, design rationale.
- Completed issues: title, owner, PR link, author, reviewer, what changed.
- Test strategy, including untestable changes and why.
- AI tool usage per member: tools, session count, AI log folder link, and 2–3 sentences on lessons
  learned.
- Release: tag and release link.
- Risks and retrospective: what worked, what slowed the team down, next-sprint changes.
- Next sprint plan: initial ideas and carryover issues.
- From Sprint 2: Sprint 1 carryovers (which were taken, which were skipped and why), and D6 and D7
  in the deliverables summary. The report covers this sprint's work only.

# AI assistance disclosure — required format

Course rule, not an upstream Gitea one. Every contributor discloses their own AI use per issue,
**even when no AI was used**. Source: the course AI Log Instructions page and `CONTRIBUTING.md`
(AI Contribution Policy). Two separate places, both required. The rest of the PR and issue
format is in `COURSE-WORKFLOW.md`.

## 1. A comment on the issue

Posted by each contributor on the **issue** they worked, once their work is done. One comment per
person — never edit someone else's. Add later sessions by editing your own table.

```markdown
### AI Assistance — @your-github-username

**Role in this issue:** Implementation

| # | Tool | Log | What AI helped with |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | claude-code | [2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/blob/main/ai-logs/sprint1/YourName/2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl.md) | Confirmed the files found during concept location, drafted the template change and tests, ran them |

**Attachments:** [2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl/](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/tree/main/ai-logs/sprint1/YourName/2026-09-24_claude-code_issue-52-impl)
```

- **Role** is one of Implementation, Code review, Testing, Other — pick the ones that apply and
  delete the rest, do not leave the slash list in place.
- **Tool** is the tool's name, e.g. `claude-code`, `claude-web`.
- **Log** is a full `https://github.com/...` link to the filed log. Relative paths break in issue
  comments. File naming is in `ai-logs/README.md`.
- **Attachments** only when the log has a companion folder; otherwise drop the line.
- **No AI used?** Keep the heading and role line and write `No AI used` in place of the table.

## 2. A short section in the pull request description — no log link

Reviewers read the PR, and the review rubric scores "AI transparency", so the PR says how AI was
used and how you verified it. It does **not** link or cite the AI log: from Sprint 1 on, logs are
referenced in **issue comments only**, never in PR descriptions or PR comments (Sprint 1 page, D5).

```markdown
## AI assistance

Claude Code (claude-opus-5) drafted the handler and tests following the existing register/delete
code; I reviewed every line, ran the tests, checked the page by hand, and can explain each change.
AI log: see the AI Assistance comment on the linked issue.
```

Name the model, say what AI did and what you did, and point at the issue comment for the log.

## Rules that make a disclosure wrong

- **Placeholders left in**: `@your-github-username` or the full `Implementation / Code review /
  Testing / Other` list means the comment was pasted unread.
- **A log link in a PR description or PR comment.** Log links live in the issue comment only.
- **A log link that 404s.** Until the log is merged to `main`, link the branch that holds it; switch
  to the `main` link once merged.
- **A log folder that is not your GitHub username** — `ai-logs/sprint1/jdonohue/` is wrong when the
  account is `Jack-Donohue`.
- **Claiming work AI did as your own, or the reverse.** The claim must match the log.
- **AI-written replies to reviewer questions on your own issue or PR.** `CONTRIBUTING.md` forbids it:
  the questions are for you.

## For AI agents drafting an issue or PR

Put section 2 in every PR description you draft, and draft the section 1 issue comment
separately, both filled in from the session you actually ran — never with placeholders. You may
draft the wording, but say plainly that the human must review and edit it before posting, and leave
the issue comment for them to post under their own account.

### Code Review — @vvchopra

**Checked:** Read the full diff against `main` (Go replay and queries, route and permissions, Vue
component, utils, locale strings, tests) and traced the replay by hand for items that leave the
milestone, closed milestones and toggle round-trips. I have not yet run the tests or the page
locally. <!-- TODO before posting: run `go test ./models/issues/ ./services/issue/` and
`pnpm exec vitest RepoMilestoneBurndown`, open a milestone page, and update this line -->

| Criterion | Score (1–10) | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correctness — implements issue requirements | 7 | All ten ACs are addressed. Edge cases found: (R1) a closed milestone's chart runs past its close date when an item that already left it is closed later; (R2) toggling "Include pull requests" twice quickly can show data that doesn't match the checkbox; (R3) a viewer who can read PRs but not issues sees "no issues or pull requests yet" by default. |
| Test coverage — tests present and meaningful | 8 | Strong: a pure calculation with 23 table cases, permission tests confirmed to fail without the check, vitest and e2e. Missing a case for R1 (item leaves, then closes after the milestone closes) and a far-off projection (O2). |
| Code quality — style, naming, no duplication | 8 | Clean, well commented, with tight queries. Optional: skip zero-count deltas in `replayMilestoneItem` (fixes R1 at the root), and count `Added`/`Removed` from `Changes` instead of tracking both. |
| Documentation — comments and PR description clear | 9 | Very thorough. The PR maps every AC, and the deliberate departures from the issue are explained. Course docs and their guide twins are updated. |
| AI transparency — evidence of human verification if AI used | 8 | The AI section says what the AI did and what the author decided, including catching three missed ACs. It doesn't say which results the author checked personally, apart from approving commits. |
| Overall — merge as-is? | 7 | Merge after R1–R3. The optional items can follow later. |

**Required**

- **R1** `services/issue/milestone_burndown.go` `replayMilestoneItem`: a close or reopen while the
  item is outside the milestone still produces a (zero-count) delta. `CalcMilestoneBurndown` then
  does `end = max(ClosedDateUnix, deltas[last].at)`, so a milestone closed on Mar 1 whose former
  item closed on Jun 1 charts flat through June. Only append a delta when `remaining != 0 || scope != 0`.
  That also stops `lastAt` from picking up unrelated events.
- **R2** `RepoMilestoneBurndown.vue` `fetchBurndown`: overlapping requests aren't sequenced, so a
  slower `include_pulls=1` response can land after the user unticks the box. Drop superseded
  responses (request counter or `AbortController`).
- **R3** `routers/web/repo/milestone.go` `MilestoneBurndownData`: if the viewer can't read issues
  (e.g. the issues unit is off), both kinds are off by default and the chart says the milestone is
  empty. Default to pull requests in that case, or pre-tick the box.

**Optional**

- **O1** If a refetch fails, the header keeps the previous summary next to the "failed" title.
  Clear `burndown` or hide the summary on error.
- **O2** The projection isn't capped like the due date (`burndownHorizonDays`). A slow burn
  (e.g. 100 left, 1 closed in 14 days → about 4 years) stretches the axis and squashes the history.
- **O3** `projected_on_time` / `projected_late` read "1 days" when the difference is one day.
- **O4** An issue transferred to another repo disappears from every past day, because the queries
  filter on its current `repo_id`. Probably fine to leave as a known limitation, but worth a line
  in the PR.

feat(shortcut): g shortcuts for the repository tabs and notifications ab-wm feat/issue-58-g-shortcuts open False
Closes #58

## What changed and why

GitHub users move around a repository with two-key `g` shortcuts, and Gitea had none. Building on #56's registry, this PR adds them: `g c`, `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` go to a repository's Code, Issues, Pull Requests, Actions and Wiki tabs, and `g n` goes to the user's notifications from any page.

- **A link can declare its own shortcut.** A link in a template that carries a few attributes registers a shortcut that goes where the link leads. The shortcut only exists while the link is on the page, so it follows whatever the template already decides about the link.
- **The tab bar declares the repository shortcuts.** Each tab marks itself, so a tab that isn't shown (its feature is turned off, the user can't read it, or it is Actions on an empty repository) has no shortcut. The external issue tracker and external wiki tabs aren't marked, so a shortcut never leaves Gitea. Tabs that move into the "more" menu on a narrow window are still on the page, so their shortcuts keep working.
- **`g c` goes to the repository's front page,** not where the Code tab links: on a branch other than the default, the Code tab points at that branch.
- **`g n` is declared on the notifications bell,** which only signed-in users have. The bell is in the page twice, once for phones and once for desktops, so only one copy declares it.
- **Each shortcut is listed with its tab's translated name** ("Issues", without the open count), in the "Repository" section with `s` and `t`. `g n` is "Notifications" under a new "General" string, which #57's help dialog will also use for `?`.
- The docs in `.claude-students` are updated with the new way to add a shortcut.

## How the changes relate to the ACs

- **AC1:** `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` on a repository page go to that tab.
- **AC2:** `g c` goes to the repository's front page on the default branch, even while browsing another branch.
- **AC3:** a tab that is not shown declares no shortcut, so its keys do nothing.
- **AC4:** the external tracker and wiki tabs declare no shortcut, so `g i` and `g w` do nothing there and the browser stays in Gitea.
- **AC5:** tabs in the "more" menu are still on the page, so their shortcuts work.
- **AC6:** signed in, `g n` goes to notifications from any page; signed out there is no bell, so it does nothing.
- **AC7:** outside a repository there is no tab bar, so the repository shortcuts do nothing.
- **AC8:** each repository shortcut has its tab's name in the Repository section, and `g n` is "Notifications" under "General".

## How it was tested

### Test strategy

Most of the risk in this PR is in the wiring, not the code: whether a shortcut exists is decided by the templates, so most mistakes only show up on a real page. The tests are split along that line.

- **Unit tests (Vitest) for the part that is plain code.** Turning a link into a shortcut needs no server, so it is tested on its own, where the tests are fast and a failure points straight at the cause. The 4 new tests in `web_src/js/modules/shortcut.test.ts` target the three places where the obvious version would be wrong: a description taken from the link's text would include the open count, following the link would keep `g c` on the browsed branch, and treating a hidden link as gone would break the "more" menu. They are named `#58 AC…`, because the other tests in that file use #56's AC numbers.
- **Playwright tests for the wiring.** A unit test can't see which tabs a template renders. Each of the 4 new tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` sets up the one situation where a wiring mistake would show: a branch other than the default, the only time `g c` and the Code tab disagree; turned-off and external tabs, the only time a shortcut could outlive its tab or leave Gitea; a narrow window, the only time tabs move; and a signed-in user, the only time there are two bells to clash. On an ordinary page each of these mistakes would pass unnoticed. A new `apiEditRepo` helper in `tests/e2e/utils.ts` sets up the repository with the turned-off and external tabs.
- **Proving that nothing happened.** A test that presses a dead shortcut and sees nothing would also pass on a page where no key works at all. The AC3 and AC4 test therefore presses a live shortcut (`s`) after the dead ones and checks that it still runs.

**Testing the tests.** Each test was checked via mutation testing to ensure that the tests actually detect something real. For the unit tests: taking the description from the link's text, dropping the section, an action that does nothing, ignoring a link's own address, and treating a hidden part of the page as gone. For the Playwright tests: the Code tab without its own address, a shortcut on the external tracker tab, both bells declaring `g n`, and treating hidden elements as gone. Each break failed the matching tests, and #56's tests stayed green.

**Not covered automatically, and why.** AC3's other cases, a tab the user can't read and Actions on an empty repository, aren't driven separately. The template hides those tabs the same way it hides a turned-off one, which the AC3 test covers.

**Checked by hand.** Claude also drove a headless browser through a local instance: the tab shortcuts, `g c` from a branch, a narrow window, and `g n` signed in and out. I spot checked the shortcuts myself as well.

| AC | What the tests check |
| --- | --- |
| AC1 | `g i`, `g p`, `g a` and `g w` each go to their tab on a real repository; a link's shortcut goes where the link leads |
| AC2 | On a branch other than the default, the Code tab links to that branch and `g c` goes to the front page; a link's shortcut can go to its own address |
| AC3 | With pull requests and Actions turned off, no `g p` or `g a` is declared, the keys do nothing and a live shortcut still runs after them |
| AC4 | With an external tracker and wiki, their tabs are shown but declare nothing, the keys do nothing and no new tab opens |
| AC5 | At 420 px wide the Wiki tab is in the "more" menu and `g w` still works; a link moved into a hidden part of the page keeps its shortcut |
| AC6 | Signed out there is no `g n`; signed in there is exactly one, and it goes to notifications |
| AC7 | On `/explore/repos` no repository shortcut is declared |
| AC8 | Issues is "Issues" in "Repository", and `g n` is "Notifications" in "General"; a link is listed with its own description, not its text |

## CI / manual verification

- CI runs on the PR; per the course rules, it must pass before merging.
- `make test-frontend`: 361 tests pass, including the 4 new ones.
- `make lint-js`, `make lint-templates`, `make lint-editorconfig` and the locale JSON lint pass.
- The 7 Playwright tests in `tests/e2e/shortcut.test.ts` pass locally on Chromium and Firefox; each new one runs in under 1.5 s.
- `./.claude-students/check.sh` reports only the two `models-issues.md` size limits, which were failing before this PR.

## Design

Design decisions noted under issue #58.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- `g n` and the tabs in the "more" menu rely on #56 counting a hidden element as present. The bell that declares `g n` is the phone-layout copy, which is hidden on desktops, and tabs in the closed "more" menu are hidden too. If the registry ever started ignoring hidden elements, as #56's Tech Debt suggests later shortcuts might need, both would stop working. The Playwright tests for AC5 and AC6 fail if that happens.

**Encountered:**
- The navbar renders its icons, the notifications bell among them, twice: once for the phone layout and once for desktop, with CSS hiding one. For a signed-in user both copies are in the page, unless they must change their password first, so marking both with `g n` makes #56's registry throw a clash on every page. Handled by a `WithShortcut` flag that only the copy rendered for every signed-in user passes. The core issue of two notification bells was not fixed here.

## Implementation Note
Despite the changes impacting the user-facing experience, there are no UI changes that require before and after screenshots. As confusing as this may be, these shortcuts only take the user to another page, and don't add, remove or change any element on the page.

=====
`g` navigation shortcuts for repository tabs and notifications
> Blocked by #56, which adds the shortcut registry these shortcuts are built on.

## User Story

As a Gitea user who knows GitHub's keyboard shortcuts, I want the same two-key `g` shortcuts to perform the same behavior, taking me to a repository's code, issues, pull requests, actions and wiki, and to my notifications, so that I can move around without reaching for the mouse.

## User Scenario
A reviewer is reading a file on a feature branch. They press `g` then `i` and land on the repository's issue list, then `g` then `p` for the pull request list. Pressing `g` then `c` takes them back to the repository's front page on its default branch, the same as on GitHub. From anywhere in Gitea, while signed in, `g` then `n` opens their notifications.

A shortcut only works when its tab is shown. On a repository with the wiki turned off, or one that uses an external wiki, pressing `g` then `w` does nothing at all: no navigation, no error.

| Keys | Goes to | Works when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `g c` | The repository's front page, default branch | The Code tab is shown |
| `g i` | Issues | Gitea's own issue tracker is shown |
| `g p` | Pull requests | The Pull requests tab is shown |
| `g a` | Actions | The Actions tab is shown |
| `g w` | Wiki | Gitea's own wiki is shown |
| `g n` | Notifications | The user is signed in (any page) |

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] AC1: Given a page inside a repository, when the user presses `g` then `i`, `p`, `a` or `w`, then the browser goes to that repository's Issues, Pull requests, Actions or Wiki tab.
- [ ] AC2: Given a page inside a repository while browsing a branch other than the default, when the user presses `g` then `c`, then the browser goes to the repository's front page on its default branch, even though the Code tab itself links to the branch being browsed.
- [ ] AC3: Given a tab that is not shown (its unit is disabled, the user cannot read it, or it is Actions on an empty repository), when the user presses its shortcut, then nothing happens and the page does not navigate.
- [ ] AC4: Given a repository that uses an external issue tracker or an external wiki, when the user presses `g i` or `g w`, then nothing happens and the browser never leaves Gitea.
- [ ] AC5: Given a narrow window where some tabs have moved into the tab bar's "more" menu, when the user presses one of their shortcuts, then it still works.
- [ ] AC6: Given any page while signed in, when the user presses `g` then `n`, then the browser goes to the notifications page; when signed out, nothing happens.
- [ ] AC7: Given a page outside any repository, when the user presses a repository shortcut such as `g i`, then nothing happens.
- [ ] AC8: Given the shortcuts on a page, when they are listed, then each repository shortcut is described by its tab's translated name (for example "Issues", without the open count) and is in the repository section, and `g n` is "Notifications" in the site-wide section.

## Out of Scope
- GitHub shortcuts for tabs Gitea does not have: Discussions (`g g`) and Security (`g s`).
- Shortcuts for tabs GitHub has no shortcut for: Releases, Projects, Packages, Activity and Settings.
- Other site-wide shortcuts, such as GitHub's `s` or `/` to focus the top search bar.
- Shortcuts that act on the current page instead of navigating, such as closing an issue or assigning labels.
- Showing the shortcuts to the user: Issue (#57)
- Changing what the tab bar shows or where its tabs link.

## Open Questions
None

## Design Decisions
Added per commit during implementation, as in #53 and #54.

## Scope
medium (3 points)

import {registerGlobalInitFunc} from './observer.ts';
import {hideElem, toggleElem} from '../utils/dom.ts';

const sequenceTimeoutMs = 1500; // the longest wait between the keys of a sequence

export type Shortcut = {
  keys: string, // keys pressed one after another, separated by spaces, e.g. "g c"
  description: string, // translated
  section?: string, // translated
  element?: HTMLElement, // the shortcut only exists while this element is in the document
  action: () => void,
};

export type ShortcutInfo = Pick<Shortcut, 'keys' | 'description' | 'section'>;

function isActive(shortcut: Shortcut): boolean {
  return !shortcut.element || shortcut.element.isConnected;
}

// returns the shortcut for exactly these keys, 'prefix' if they start a longer sequence, or null
function matchKeys(shortcuts: Shortcut[], keys: string): Shortcut | 'prefix' | null {
  for (const shortcut of shortcuts) {
    if (shortcut.keys === keys) return shortcut;
    if (shortcut.keys.startsWith(`${keys} `)) return 'prefix';
  }
  return null;
}

export class ShortcutRegistry {
  private shortcuts: Shortcut[] = [];
  private pendingKeys = ''; // the start of a sequence pressed so far
  private pendingTime = 0;

  register(shortcut: Shortcut) {
    const keys = shortcut.keys.trim().split(/\s+/).join(' ').toLowerCase(); // "g  c" would otherwise never match a press
    // a shortcut whose element has left the page, e.g. a hint replaced by file tree navigation, gives way to the new one
    this.shortcuts = this.shortcuts.filter(isActive);
    const conflict = this.shortcuts.find((s) => s.keys === keys || s.keys.startsWith(`${keys} `) || keys.startsWith(`${s.keys} `));
    if (conflict) throw new Error(`Keyboard shortcut "${keys}" conflicts with "${conflict.keys}"`);
    this.shortcuts.push({...shortcut, keys});
  }

  list(): ShortcutInfo[] {
    return this.shortcuts.filter(isActive).map(({keys, description, section}) => ({keys, description, section}));
  }

  handleKeyDown(e: KeyboardEvent) {
    const target = e.target as HTMLElement;
    // the key was already used by a widget such as a menu, or is being typed into a field
    if (e.defaultPrevented || e.ctrlKey || e.metaKey || e.altKey || target.matches('input, textarea, select') || target.isContentEditable) {
      this.pendingKeys = '';
      return;
    }
    if (e.key === 'Shift') return; // not a press of its own, e.g. on the way to "?"
    if (e.repeat) return; // a held key runs its shortcut once, and doesn't start over after a sequence

    if (Date.now() - this.pendingTime > sequenceTimeoutMs) this.pendingKeys = '';
    const key = e.key.toLowerCase();
    const shortcuts = this.shortcuts.filter(isActive);
    let keys = this.pendingKeys ? `${this.pendingKeys} ${key}` : key;
    let match = matchKeys(shortcuts, keys);
    if (!match && keys !== key) {
      // the key does not continue the sequence, so it acts as a fresh press
      keys = key;
      match = matchKeys(shortcuts, keys);
    }
    this.pendingKeys = '';
    if (!match) return;

    e.preventDefault();
    if (match === 'prefix') {
      this.pendingKeys = keys;
      this.pendingTime = Date.now();
    } else {
      match.action();
    }
  }
}

const globalRegistry = new ShortcutRegistry();

// Adds a keyboard shortcut to the page. Throws if the keys clash with an existing shortcut.
export function registerShortcut(shortcut: Shortcut) {
  globalRegistry.register(shortcut);
}

// The shortcuts available on the current page, e.g. for a help dialog
export function getShortcuts(): ShortcutInfo[] {
  return globalRegistry.list();
}

export function initShortcutKbd(kbd: HTMLElement) {
  // Handle initial state: hide the kbd hint if the associated input already has a value
  // (e.g., from browser autofill or back/forward navigation cache)
  const elem = elemFromKbd(kbd)!;
  if (elem.value) hideElem(kbd);
  kbd.setAttribute('aria-hidden', 'true');
  kbd.setAttribute('aria-keyshortcuts', kbd.getAttribute('data-shortcut-keys')!);
  registerShortcut({
    keys: kbd.getAttribute('data-shortcut-keys')!,
    description: elem.placeholder,
    section: kbd.getAttribute('data-shortcut-section') ?? undefined,
    element: kbd,
    action: () => elem.focus(),
  });

--- ab-wm 2026-10-20T01:17:54Z 
 ## Design Decisions - @ab-wm

### Decisions for Commit 1
#### Decision 1: Each tab's link in the tab bar declares its own `g` shortcut

**Decision:** The tab bar's links declare their shortcuts in the page's HTML, and a shortcut goes where its link leads. The one exception is `g c`, which goes to the repository's front page instead of the branch the Code tab points at. The notifications bell declares `g n` the same way.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) The server works out which tabs the user may open and hands the page a list of their addresses. (b) The page code builds each address from the repository's address, for example by adding `/issues`.
**Rationale:** The tab bar already decides which tabs to show. It leaves out a tab whose feature is turned off, one the user cannot read, and Actions on an empty repository, and it shows an outside link for an external tracker or wiki. Declaring the shortcut on the tab means a shortcut exists exactly when its tab does, so AC3, AC4 and AC7 need no rules of their own. (a) would repeat the tab bar's rules in a second place, where they could drift apart. (b) cannot tell which tabs are shown, so it would send users to pages they cannot open, or have to look at the tab bar anyway. On a narrow window, tabs that no longer fit move into the "more" menu but stay on the page, so their shortcuts keep working (AC5).
**Consequences:** A `g` shortcut for another tab later takes a few attributes on its link. Each shortcut's description is given separately, because a tab's text also holds its open count. The bell is in the HTML twice, once for small screens and once for large ones, so only one copy declares `g n`, or the two would clash. `g c` carries its own address, because following the Code tab would keep the user on the branch they are browsing (AC2).

### Decisions for Commit 4
#### Decision 2: `g n` is listed under a new "General" heading shared with the help dialog

**Decision:** `g n` is listed as "Notifications" under a new "General" heading, kept as a new translated string that will be used by #57 as well.
**Alternatives Considered:** (a) Reuse an existing "General" string, such as the one on the settings pages. (b) List `g n` with no heading, and let the help dialog decide where shortcuts without one go.
**Rationale:** (a) needs no new string, but borrows text translators wrote for the settings pages, so a language that words that tab differently would carry it into the shortcut list. (b) needs no new string either, but `?` would be under "General" while `g n` had no heading, so the dialog would need a rule its spec does not state, and "the site-wide section" in AC8 would come down to interpretation. A shared string gives one heading and one translation, and the list of shortcuts itself says that `g n` and `?` belong together.
**Consequences:** #58 adds one new string for #57 to reuse, so it adds a small hurdle of communication to ensure one's changes do not compete with another's. Shortcuts that work on ever

_**Agent (claude-opus-5-5 2026-10-22 15:27:02Z)**_

In [PR #73](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea/pull/73), "Due soon" means a due date from **one second after now up to 72 hours from now**. Both ends are included.

The filter code at `routers/web/shared/issue/issue_due_date.go:33` sets the window like this:

```go
case "soon":
    f.AfterUnix = now.Unix() + 1
    f.BeforeUnix = now.Add(issues_model.NearDueDuration).Unix()
```

`NearDueDuration` is `72 * time.Hour`, defined in `models/issues/deadline.go:15`. It's the same constant behind the "near due" badge on issues, so the filter and the badge always agree.

**In practice:** Gitea stores every due date as 23:59:59 local time. So "Due soon" covers deadlines on today and the next two calendar days.
- **Example:** at Wednesday 3:30 PM, the window runs to Saturday 3:30 PM. Wednesday, Thursday and Friday deadlines match. Saturday's deadline (23:59:59) falls just outside.
- **Overdue items are excluded**, because the window starts after now.
- **Open/closed state doesn't matter:** one integration test confirms a closed issue matches on its due date alone.

# Mid-Sprint Check-in: @ab-wm
## Question 1: What did you implement so far in the sprint, and what remains?
So far, I have one issue (#56) that has been closed and its PR (#96) merged in. I have one issue that will be tentatively closed with the eventual merge of PR #97. Since the first issue was a medium issue worth five points, and the second issue a medium with 3 points, I decided to implement another small issue to reach a total of 10 points.

The last issue, which adds more shortcut behaviors, has actually already been implemented and its PR drafted, but this is on a completely separate git-worktree in the specstory folder. This is because I wanted to wait for the merging of the PRs before I created a new branch. Once the PR #96 is merged into main, I will cherry pick those commits into a new branch, which conviniently gives me an another chance to review the changes in each commit.

There is nothing else of note that is left to be done, other than ensuring my AI-logs have been uploaded, the links to them are updated, and any other things I may have forgotten.

## Question 2: What is ont thing you learned about the codebase or about software engineering practice?
The backend changes for the first medium sized issue I implemented really showacased the extent to which the code has been fragmented and responsibility spread everywhere. Previous to the implementation, every implementation of a shortcut had to be specifically defined at every location that it wanted to be used. Thus, there was no way to cleanly monitor clashes, the same shortcut keys kept getting implemented over and over in different places, and no central location to register or monitor the behavior of shortcuts. After the implementation, there is finally a central location through where the behavior is established and processed.

When it comes to the concept of software engineering itself, the use of AI really forced me to reckon with what is needed and what is not. Issue splitting and ACs were too specific / complicated, and feature implementations added more changes that were needed. Controlling AI meant me unknowingly following the YAGNI ("You aren't gonna need it", part of extreme programming) concept to direct the AI agent to implement features to the defined extent, reduce side-effecting behavior, and be realistic on requirements and the end goals of an issue.

## Question 3: What is one thing you would do differently?
I am not too sure how to respond to this question. A major part of my workflow has been established through the exprience from the previous sprints, such as how I control my AI agents. how I frame my PR's and issues, how do I review changes that AI implements e.t.c. I have managed to make this as efficient as possible that I would have 2 agents running at the same time doing different tasks, speeding up my efficiency.

If there is one aspect I would like to improve, that would be organizing my work. I use two different devices, and since I do not sync anything about claude to the cloud, I do not have access to the same agents that worked on a certain concept. This is a problem, as many of these agents have 100ks of tokens of context and is better suited to answer follow up problems (like reviews). It is often the case that a review overblows an issue, or make assumptions of requirements, and an agent that is already familiar with the implementation is better suited to answer it. I am looking into seeing if I can expose my home device to the internet, safely, so I can ssh into it so I can have access to those agents.
====

# Sprint 2 Mid-Check In: @vvchopra

## What did you implement so far in the sprint, and what remains?

So far, I have split a large issue (#36) into 4 sub-issues using the INVEST format. These are 3 medium issues, and 1 small one. I have assigned the first two issues to myself (#98, #100), and have become familiarized with what the tasks involve and have a general idea of what changes will occur in the code. As of right now, I have not started the implementation of these issues, but expect to soon, followed by creating the UML diagrams along with these issues. I have also done a code review on one of my teammates' raised PRs, I expect to do a couple more code reviews once my teammates raise their PRs.

## What is one thing you learned about the codebase or about software engineering practice?

When creating an issue, it is definitely very helpful to break it down into the different requirements of User Story, Scenario, Acceptance Criteria, Out of Scope, Open Questions, and Design Decisions along with alternatives, rationale, and consequences. This is because it makes it far easier to understand what the issue involves from a short scan of the description. When delegating these issues among team members, I realize that it is important to make these issues as clear as possible in what they are doing, and how they connect to other PRs if applicable, like the 4 I created from the large issue. This makes the tasks more clear and provides direction for the implementer to work off of. Using AI to help simplify problems and understand the goals is also very important in providing clarity.

## What is one thing you would do differently?

One thing I would do differently is start the implementation slightly sooner. But, there is still a week left in the sprint and I am ready to start at this moment as I have my issues assigned, which is a better position than I was in for the last sprint. I don't expect this sprint to take much longer than the last one, as most of the requirements are fairly similar, except for the diagrams. That being said, starting sooner will leave time to make clear diagrams and understand the codebase better prior to completing the sprint. The past week has been extremely busy because of midterms, but I expect that the next week will be more calm, and I can put more focus into my implementations in the sprint.
